summary: Help children aged 5–7 describe a simple ocean food chain: tiny plants (phytoplankton) → small animals (krill/small fish) → bigger fish → top predator (shark). The two core goals are (1) understanding that this ocean food chain STARTS with tiny plants that make their own food from sunlight, and (2) reading the arrow correctly as 'is eaten by' so food/energy flows up the chain toward the eater. A central proposed activity is to have children build a chain from cards, then remove a link to notice that every animal depends on the one below it.
misconceptions: Arrow reversal: reading the arrow as 'eats' rather than 'is eaten by' — the dominant error in food-chain teaching.
'Ocean food chains start with a big animal' — missing that they start with tiny plants/plankton because those aren't obvious.
'Big/scary animals are the most important' — not seeing that predators depend on everything below them.
Believing the sea has no plants ('there's nothing green down there') so children can't locate the producer.
Thinking each animal eats only one thing / the chain is the whole story (the web extension corrects this later).

activities.title: Build-and-break the ocean food chain
steps: Take a set of picture cards — phytoplankton (tiny sea plants), krill or small fish, a bigger fish (e.g. mackerel), and a shark — and arrange them into who-eats-whom order along a lane.
Place the tiny plants first and say aloud why the chain starts there ('the plants make their own food from sunlight').

Draw or place an arrow between each pair and read the chain aloud in the arrow direction, saying 'is eaten by' at each arrow (phytoplankton is eaten by the small fish, which is eaten by the big fish, which is eaten by the shark).
Remove one card (for example the small fish) and talk through what happens to the animals that depended on it — which ones no longer have food?
activities.insight: This ocean food chain begins with tiny plants that make their own food from sunlight, and each animal depends on the one before it; the arrow means 'is eaten by' and shows food/energy travelling up toward the eater.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal predator and prey
steps: Look at a pre-drawn ocean food chain with labelled 'is eaten by' arrows.
Tap each animal to reveal what it eats and what eats it, then say the relationship aloud ('the mackerel eats the small fish and is eaten by the shark').
Point along the chain and say which way the food/energy travels.
activities.insight: The producer (phytoplankton) makes its own food and has nothing below it; each animal above the base has prey below it, and every animal except the top predator also has a predator above it. The arrow consistently points to the eater.

activities.title: Order the chain and explain the arrow
steps: Put the pictures in order: phytoplankton → small fish → big fish → shark.
Answer: what does this ocean food chain start with?
Answer: what does the arrow between two animals mean, and which way does it point?
activities.insight: Confirms the child can both sequence the chain producer-first and state that the arrow means 'is eaten by', pointing to the eater.

activities.title: What-if dependence talk (optional companion)
steps: With a built chain in front of them, discuss: 'If there were no phytoplankton at all, what would happen to the little animals, then the fish, then the shark?'
Discuss 'Which is more important to the whole chain — the shark or the tiny plants? Why?'

If a marine expert or knowledgeable adult is available, ask curiosity questions like 'what does a shark eat, and what does that eat?' and be nudged to keep tracing down until they name the plant at the bottom.
activities.insight: Removing the producer collapses everything above it, so the tiny plants — not the biggest animal — underpin the whole chain; this seeds later food-web work.

checkQuestion: Here is an ocean food chain someone made: they put the SHARK first because it's the biggest and strongest, then a fish, then tiny sea plants (phytoplankton) last. Is that the right way round? Tell me what should come FIRST in the chain and why, and what the arrows between them mean.
checkAnswer: It's the wrong way round. The chain should START with the tiny sea plants (phytoplankton), because they make their own food from sunlight and everything else depends on them. Then small animals eat the phytoplankton, bigger fish eat the small animals, and the shark (a top predator) comes LAST. The arrows point from the food to the eater (phytoplankton → small animal → fish → shark) and mean 'is eaten by' — they show which way the food/energy goes.
